title: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Form of small organisms is set by surface tension, not gravity, favouring spheres

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity and mainly due to surface tension, acting either now or at an earlier stage before the form was made rigid, so small organisms tend strongly toward spherical and other simple surface-tension forms that do not occur in the external form of large animals.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In like manner we shall find that the form of all small organisms is largely independent of gravity, and largely if not mainly due to the force of surface-tension

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Surface tension rules small organisms”. Scope: small organisms and individual cells versus large animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.46

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The gravity-versus-tension prediction can be formalized and tested in selected cells or microorganisms. Public imaging is abundant but force metadata and taxonomic breadth are insufficient for the universal mechanistic claim.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across organism sizes, quantify deviation from spherical or capillary-equilibrium shapes and compare estimated capillary and gravitational stresses using Bond numbers and perturbation data. Small forms insensitive to gravity but predictably altered by interfacial or cortical tension would support the mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Active cytoskeletal forces can mimic tension-driven shapes.

All small organisms is an exceptionally broad scope.

Most datasets lack measured tension and gravity perturbations.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.45
operationalizability: 0.65
data existence: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.5

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Sphericity versus size is measurable on existing images, and large-animal external form is obviously not a surface-tension minimum, so part of the contrast can be checked. The causal attribution is a reinterpretation, and spheres have several mechanical explanations, so shape catalogs do not cleanly favor surface tension over those rivals. Coverage of the smallest organisms is patchy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Score sphericity, or departure from a constant-mean-curvature shape, against body or cell size, and compare gravitational stress with a surface-stress estimate. Small organisms clustering on those simple shapes, and large animals' external forms not doing so, would support the descriptive half; assigning the cause to surface tension rather than a wall or cytoskeleton requires the force comparison.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Walls, internal pressure, and cortical tension produce spherical outlines without classical surface tension.

Image collections over-represent model cells rather than a size gradient of whole organisms.
